<reason>Both sides executed at a high level with clean format compliance, direct A1/A2 answers, and sustained clash. B's two strongest routes — the island-category vs. risk-criterion mismatch and the enforceability of outvoted text — were genuinely damaging, but A answered both under pressure: the annihilation-vs-injury statehood distinction (A4.1) coherently tied the category to the motion's own "existential risk" language, and the "price of defiance / authored baseline" mechanism plus the observation that ambitious text never survives consensus gave A a live counter to B's self-enforcement argument that B never fully closed. A's meta-response that every voting formula is chosen after its winners are known blunted B's "rigging" charge, and the Paris-withdrawal example undercut B's consent mechanism. B's "authorship without enforcement" and visible-blocking-vs-invisible-defiance points kept this competitive to the final word, but A made the debate slightly easier to decide by resolving more of B's pressure than B resolved of A's. Razor-thin-to-clear edge to PRO on argument resolution and closing weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The category-vs-criterion clash: B's B2.1-B2.2 dilemma (weight only islands = arbitrary; weight all at-risk states = islands swamped) was the sharpest attack of the debate, and A's A4.1 answer — defining existential risk as risk to statehood itself, making total submergence the limiting case rather than a rigged carve-out — was the most decisive resolution, then capped by A5.1's point that every voting formula is chosen after its winners are known.</best_rebuttal>
